title: My family
goal: Name family members, use possessives that follow the noun's gender, and give ages with numbers up to a hundred.
bekal: use *mój / moja / moje* and their twins for every person
ask and answer *ile masz lat?* correctly
see why ages sometimes take *lata* and sometimes *lat*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Zdjęcie rodzinne
dialogs.intro: The dorm common room. Ania opens the photo gallery on her phone.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: To jest moja rodzina. Chcesz zobaczyć zdjęcie?
lines.id: This is my family. Do you want to see a photo?
lines.literal: this is my family. you-want see photo?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: To moi rodzice. Tata ma pięćdziesiąt lat, a mama czterdzieści osiem.
lines.id: These are my parents. Dad is fifty, and Mom is forty-eight.
lines.literal: these my parents. dad has fifty years, and mom forty eight.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And the girl next to them?

lines.text: To moja siostra Kasia. Ma dwadzieścia dwa lata i studiuje medycynę.
lines.id: That's my sister Kasia. She's twenty-two and studies medicine.
lines.literal: this my sister Kasia. has twenty two years and studies medicine.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Tak, mam starszego brata. Nazywa się Piotr i jest żonaty.
lines.id: Yes, I have an older brother. His name is Piotr and he's married.
lines.literal: yes, I-have older brother. names self Piotr and is married.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A ja mam dwie siostry i jednego brata.

lines.literal: and I have two-f sisters and one brother.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Duża rodzina! Ile lat ma twój brat?
lines.id: A big family! How old is your brother?
lines.literal: big family! how-many years has your brother?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma szesnaście lat. Jeszcze chodzi do szkoły.
lines.id: He's sixteen. He's still at school.
lines.literal: has sixteen years. still walks to school.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: And you? How old are you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mam dwadzieścia trzy lata. Tęsknię za rodziną.
lines.id: I'm twenty-three. I miss my family.
lines.literal: I-have twenty three years. I-miss after family.

notes: **Ile masz lat?** literally "how many years do you have". Polish **has** an age; it doesn't *be* an age like English. The answer uses *mam* too: *mam dwadzieścia trzy lata*.

**Lata or lat?** Both mean "years". *Lata* comes after numbers ending in 2, 3, 4 (*dwa lata*, *dwadzieścia trzy lata*); *lat* after other numbers (*pięć lat*, *szesnaście lat*, *pięćdziesiąt lat*). The full rule is in the second grammar box.

**Moi rodzice** — not *moje*. Possessives have their own form for groups that **include men**: *moi*. The pattern you saw in *ci studenci* (Unit 3) and *wszyscy* (Unit 4) shows up here again, and will keep showing up.
**Rodzice** means "parents" and is always plural — there's no singular form. For one parent, use *tata* or *mama*.

**Mam brata, mam starszego brata.** Why *brata*, not *brat*? Because it's the **object** of the verb *mieć*, and masculine nouns for living beings change their ending as objects. That's Unit 7 — you're already seeing its shadow.
**Dwie siostry, dwa lata.** The number "two" has two faces: *dwa* for masculine and neuter words, *dwie* for feminine words. Only two behaves like this; the others have just one form.

**Chodzi do szkoły** — "walks to school", but it means "goes to school" (is a pupil). *Chodzić* is used for **repeated** actions, *iść* for what's happening right now. Pairs like this are handled in Unit 13.

**Tęsknię za rodziną** — "I miss my family". *Za* here requires the *narzędnik* form (*rodzina → rodziną*), the same form as after *jestem*. Learn it as a package: *tęsknię za domem*, *tęsknię za mamą*.

grammars.title: Possessives — they follow the thing owned
body: What decides the form is not the owner but **the thing**. "My book" and "my table" use different possessives because book and table have different genders.
after: The good news is in three rows: ***jego***, ***jej***, and ***ich*** **never change at all**. A third of this table is nothing to memorize.
Only *mój*, *twój*, *nasz*, *wasz* change — and the pattern is uniform: add **-a** for feminine, **-e** for neuter, **-i** for groups with men.
When talking about family, the possessive is often **dropped** when it's obvious: *Tata ma pięćdziesiąt lat* — "(my) dad is fifty". Saying *mój tata* every time actually sounds excessive.

grammars.title: Numbers and nouns: the 2-3-4 rule
body: The most typically Polish rule of all, and the most surprising for English speakers, who only ever switch between singular and plural.
after: The rule depends on the **last digit**, not on how big the number is. So 22, 32, 42 all behave like 2, while 12, 13, 14 do **not** — the teens always join the "five and up" group: *dwanaście lat*.
For now, two chunks you really use every day are enough: **…dwa/trzy/cztery lata** and **…lat** for the rest. The special form is called *dopełniacz* plural and comes in Unit 15.

blocks.text: Like English, Polish has no single word for "older brother" or "younger sister". To be specific, use an adjective: *starszy brat* (older brother), *młodsza siostra* (younger sister).

blocks.title: Ready-made family sentences
items: *Mam dwie siostry i jednego brata.* — I have two sisters and one brother.
*Nie mam rodzeństwa.* — I'm an only child. (literally: I have no siblings)
*Moja rodzina mieszka w Indonezji.* — My family lives in Indonesia.

blocks.text: Compound numbers are built just like in English — tens first, then units, but with no hyphen or "and": *dwadzieścia trzy* (23), *czterdzieści osiem* (48), *dziewięćdziesiąt dziewięć* (99).

blocks.title: Pronunciation tips
items: All tens from 50 up contain *-dziesiąt* — read **JYE-shont**, and it sticks tightly to its number.
*sześćdziesiąt* (60) really does look impossible. Split it into *sześć* + *dziesiąt* and it's tamed at once: sheshch-JYE-shont.
For phone numbers, Poles read the digits in groups of two or three, much as English speakers do.
